prompt: What does moving the booking system from IaaS to SaaS take off the clinic's security to-do list?
hint: Work, mostly of the kind people already did well.

choices.text: Patching the operating system and the runtime
choices.why: Right. What is left is accounts, sharing, integrations, retention, the data and the access.

choices.text: Deciding who may see the patients' records
choices.why: That item is on every list; no model removes it.

choices.text: Everything, because the vendor now secures the product and the clinic's use of it
choices.why: The vendor secures its platform; the settings inside the clinic's tenant stay the clinic's.

choices.text: Keeping the records for the time the law requires
choices.why: Retention is on the SaaS list too: a setting in the tenant, and the contract.

prompt: A function has no ports to open. Which item on the PaaS list plays the part that "which ports are open" plays on IaaS?
hint: The items change shape, not just number.

choices.text: The runtime version it runs on
choices.why: That one plays the part of the operating system's patches.

choices.text: Who is allowed to invoke it
choices.why: Right. An invocation permission can say "anybody", as a port can be open to the world.

choices.text: The libraries the code ships with, listed in its requirements
choices.why: Those play the part of the operating system's packages.

choices.text: Nothing: a function cannot be reached from outside
choices.why: It can, as soon as somebody grants an invocation permission or a public URL; lesson 13.

prompt: Which items are on the list in all three models? Choose all that apply.
hint: The last two of every list.

choices.text: The data
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Who can reach the data
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The operating system's patches
choices.why: IaaS only.

choices.text: The runtime version
choices.why: IaaS and PaaS; a rented product has no runtime of yours.

prompt: Who patches the operating system of a virtual machine the clinic launched on AWS?
hint: What has the provider promised never to do?

choices.text: AWS, as part of the hypervisor's maintenance
choices.why: The hypervisor is below the line; the machine's operating system is above it.

choices.text: Canonical, since the image is Ubuntu
choices.why: Canonical publishes the fixes; somebody has to install them on this machine.

choices.text: The clinic
choices.why: Right. Choosing a current image and keeping it patched is the first item on the IaaS list.

choices.text: Nobody needs to, because cloud machines are rebuilt every night
choices.why: Nothing rebuilds them unless the clinic arranges it.

prompt: The security group showed 22 and 443 open to `0.0.0.0/0`. Why close one of them and not the other?
hint: One is the service, the other a door to the operating system.

choices.text: 443 carries encrypted traffic and 22 does not
choices.why: SSH on 22 is encrypted too; the point is who needs to reach it.

choices.text: The booking system's users need 443; only the staff in one office need 22
choices.why: Right. So 22 names the office's address and nothing else.

choices.text: AWS charges for every port opened to the internet, and port 22 is billed at a higher rate than the web port
choices.why: There is no charge per open port; the reason is exposure.

choices.text: Port 22 cannot be reached through an internet gateway
choices.why: It can, which is why automated scanners try it on every address.

prompt: Why does requiring tokens on the metadata service, IMDSv2, protect a machine's role?
hint: A program tricked into fetching an address for somebody else.

choices.text: It encrypts the credentials so only the role's owner can read them
choices.why: The credentials are handed to the machine as before; what changed is how a program must ask.

choices.text: It makes the credentials expire after one request
choices.why: Their lifetime is unchanged.

choices.text: A program must first ask for a session token with a different kind of request, which such a tricked request does not make
choices.why: Right. That second step is what the Capital One case lacked.

choices.text: It hides the metadata service from programs running on the machine
choices.why: Programs on the machine still reach it; they need a token first.

prompt: To make the metadata service demand a session token, `modify-instance-metadata-options` sets `--http-tokens` to ___.
hint: The opposite of what it said at first.

prompt: The image was Ubuntu 14.04 from 2017. What is the fix, given that a running machine cannot change its image?
hint: The lab could not show it.

choices.text: Ask AWS support to upgrade it in place
choices.why: AWS does not log in to customers' machines.

choices.text: Close port 22, which removes the risk of an old system
choices.why: It reduces who can reach one door; the old system still runs the web service on 443.

choices.text: Launch another from a current Ubuntu, then keep up a patching routine
choices.why: Right. Both halves are on the IaaS list.

choices.text: Enable IMDSv2, which patches the image
choices.why: IMDSv2 changes how credentials are handed out; it patches nothing.

prompt: Put the steps of the IaaS section in order.
hint: Build, ask, fix, ask again.
items: open 22 and 443 to the world and launch from an old image
revoke 22 from the world and allow it from the office
list the open rules again and read the token setting
trap: Stopping after the fix is the slip; the second reading is the evidence.

prompt: On PaaS, what does the provider keep patched under your code?
hint: Within the version you chose.

choices.text: Your code's libraries, listed in requirements.txt
choices.why: Those you ship with the code, so they are yours; lesson 13.

choices.text: The operating system and the runtime, within the version you chose
choices.why: Right. Moving to the next version is yours.

choices.text: Everything, including moving to a new runtime version when the old one ends
choices.why: A version change can break your code, so the provider leaves it to you.

choices.text: Nothing: a function is a container you maintain yourself
choices.why: That is closer to IaaS; on PaaS the provider runs the platform.

prompt: moto created a function on `python3.7` without complaint. What would AWS do with the same request today?
hint: The runtime was deprecated at the end of 2023.

choices.text: Create it, and print a warning
choices.why: Past the deprecation, AWS stopped accepting new functions on it.

choices.text: Refuse it
choices.why: Right. Not run here: moto accepts it.

choices.text: Create it on python3.12 instead, silently
choices.why: AWS never changes a function's runtime for you; that would change your code's Python.

choices.text: Create it, and delete it after a grace period
choices.why: AWS does not delete functions for being old; that is exactly why old ones linger.

prompt: A function created in 2022 on `python3.7` still answers every request today. What is wrong with it, and who will tell you?
hint: The provider does not stop it.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong, since AWS would have stopped it otherwise
choices.why: AWS does not stop functions on a deprecated runtime; it stops patching the runtime.

choices.text: Its runtime gets no security patches; notices go to the account's contacts, and an inventory finds it
choices.why: Right. list-functions with the runtime column is the inventory.

choices.text: It fails on every request, so the users will tell you
choices.why: It keeps answering; that is why it is easy to miss.

choices.text: Its code is being rewritten by AWS for the new runtime
choices.why: Nobody rewrites your code for you.

prompt: Before running `update-function-configuration --runtime python3.12` on a real system, what should already have happened?
hint: A runtime change is a change of Python.

choices.text: The code tested on the new version
choices.why: Right. The request is one line; the test is the work.

choices.text: A ticket opened with AWS asking for the change
choices.why: The runtime version is yours to change; no ticket is involved.

choices.text: The function deleted and created again from scratch on the new runtime
choices.why: Updating the configuration is enough; deleting loses its permissions and history.

choices.text: Nothing, because a newer Python runs every older program unchanged
choices.why: Versions remove and change things; that is why the test comes first.

prompt: Match each IaaS question to its PaaS counterpart.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

pairs.left: which ports are open to the internet
which packages the operating system has
pairs.right: which libraries the code ships with

pairs.left: what the machine's role may do
pairs.right: what the function's role may do

prompt: A receptionist approved a calendar add-on in 2022, and it can still read her whole mailbox. Which SaaS item is that?
hint: Another product reaching in.

choices.text: Accounts
choices.why: Her account is fine; the problem is what she granted to another product.

choices.text: Retention and audit
choices.why: Those decide how long records stay and who read what.

choices.text: Integrations, a tenant setting
choices.why: Right. Whether a user may grant that by clicking "allow" is a tenant setting.

choices.text: Sharing
choices.why: Sharing is people being given files; this is a product being given access.

prompt: Under the LGPD, what does the data processing agreement make the vendor of a SaaS the clinic uses for patients' records?
hint: Someone who processes data on the clinic's behalf.

choices.text: The controller, who decides what is done with the data
choices.why: The clinic decides; the vendor processes under its instructions.

choices.text: An operador, acting only on the instructions it is given
choices.why: Right. And the list of subprocessors says who else touches the data.

choices.text: The data protection officer of the clinic
choices.why: That is a person the clinic names; a vendor is not made one by a contract.

choices.text: Nothing, since a contract cannot change anyone's role under the law
choices.why: The agreement is what sets out the vendor's role and limits.

prompt: What is the SaaS equivalent of the `describe-security-groups` transcript as evidence?
hint: Read the setting back and keep it.

choices.text: The vendor's SOC 2 report
choices.why: It covers the vendor's platform, not your tenant's settings.

choices.text: A dated screenshot of the tenant's sharing settings
choices.why: Right. The same habit: read it back, and keep the evidence.

choices.text: A command run against the vendor's API from moto
choices.why: moto imitates AWS, not SaaS products.

choices.text: The vendor's sales brochure listing its security features
choices.why: That says what the product can do, not what your tenant does.

prompt: Which of these are settings inside the clinic's SaaS tenant, and so the clinic's to decide? Choose all that apply.
hint: The table of four items.

choices.text: Whether files may be shared with anyone holding the link
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Whether users sign in through the clinic's identity provider
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Which hypervisor runs the vendor's servers
choices.why: Below the line, and the vendor's.

choices.text: Whether users may grant third-party apps access to mail
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: How the vendor patches its databases
choices.why: The vendor's platform work.

prompt: After the fixes in the IaaS section, how many rules of the security group were still open to `0.0.0.0/0`?
hint: The web port.

prompt: The clinic moves its booking system from a virtual machine to a SaaS product. dani, who left in March, still has an account in the old machine's operating system. What does the move do about her?
hint: Accounts are on every list.

choices.text: It ends her access, since the SaaS vendor checks every user against the clinic's staff list
choices.why: No vendor knows the clinic's staff list; accounts remain the clinic's item.

choices.text: Nothing by itself: the old machine still needs retiring, and her SaaS account, if one was made, needs ending too
choices.why: Right. Moving up the stack removes work, never the accounts item.

choices.text: It moves her account into the SaaS product automatically
choices.why: Accounts are not carried across by a migration unless somebody does it.

choices.text: It makes her account harmless, since a SaaS has no operating system
choices.why: The old machine's account works for as long as the machine runs.

prompt: Every security to-do list ends with the same two items: the data, and who can ___ it.
hint: A word for getting at something.

prompt: Which of the three models leaves the shortest security to-do list, and what never leaves it?
hint: The work gets lighter; the last two items stay.

choices.text: IaaS, because you control everything and so can fix everything
choices.why: Controlling more means more on your list, not less.

choices.text: PaaS; the runtime version never leaves
choices.why: A rented product has no runtime of yours at all.

choices.text: SaaS; the data and who can reach it never leave
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: They are the same, since the line does not move between models
choices.why: The line moves up with each model; that is the cloud course's drawing.
